title: A Cross-Modal Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Material Properties and Cellular Function Across Species and Perturbations
title_norm: a crossmodal synthesis of biomolecular condensate material properties and cellular function across species and perturbations
standardized_text:
This project investigates biomolecular condensates formed by phase separation to address the disconnected relationship between physical states and cellular outcomes. Condensates organize cellular processes through physical properties (such as viscosity) but the influence of molecular sequences on physical states remains unclear. The primary question asks how molecular features predict physical properties to transition the study of condensates into a predictive framework.

This retrospective project of data synthesis compiles public databases and extracts physical features to train multimodal models of machine learning. The team will apply models of deep learning and graph neural networks alongside sparse additive models and gradient boosted trees. Validation involves internal cross validation on held out datasets and replication across independent sources to create public sets of benchmarks.

The project will utilize diverse databases including PhaSepDB and AlphaFold DB alongside the Human Protein Atlas and Gene Expression Omnibus. Integration of datasets involves standardizing identifiers and mapping orthologs of species to construct a unified knowledge graph of phenotypic data. Because metrics are inconsistent, the project maps measurements to a latent physical state and corrects batch effects of images.

The twenty four month timeline includes establishing pipelines and extracting features to release the final knowledge graph and modules for training. Collaboration is necessary because the project demands expertise in physics of polymers and computer vision that exceeds any single laboratory.

The team will share findings through a public knowledge graph and open source tools of software alongside open datasets of benchmarks. The team includes physicists and biologists across stages of careers who will provide opportunities for training through workshops led by students.

abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates formed by phase separation organize cellular processes through physical properties like viscosity and elasticity, which are critical for maintaining normal cellular functions and preventing disease phenotypes across species. Currently, the lack of integration between biophysical measurements and large scale datasets leaves it unclear how molecular sequences and interaction networks quantitatively determine condensate physical states and biological outcomes. This project will determine how molecular features predict condensate physical properties across species by extracting features from cellular images and literature to train multimodal machine learning models, including graph neural networks and gradient boosted trees. The study will integrate diverse databases, including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, and the Human Protein Atlas, by standardizing identifiers and mapping orthologs to construct a unified knowledge graph linking molecular and phenotypic data. Ultimately, this research will establish a predictive framework that systematically links molecular scale features to macroscopic physical properties and cellular behaviors, transitioning condensate study from isolated observations to predictive science.

title: Emergent Principles of Organelle Contact Sites: A Synthesis of Proteomics, Imaging, and Genetic Interaction Data
title_norm: emergent principles of organelle contact sites a synthesis of proteomics imaging and genetic interaction data
standardized_text:
This study in cell biology investigates membrane contact sites to address the unknown network architectures that regulate interactions of organelles. Known tethering proteins and lipid transporters remain unintegrated across separate datasets of proteomics and imaging to explain behaviors at the system level. The primary question asks how a network of contact sites transitions the study from single genes to models at the system level.

This computational study aggregates existing public datasets to build a model of multi layer networks and a queryable knowledge graph. The team will apply hierarchical Bayesian models and fusion of similarity networks alongside algorithms for community detection to analyze the network. Validation of results involves benchmarking against established sets of genes and known complexes of proteins to ensure accuracy.

The project utilizes databases including PRIDE and the Human Protein Atlas alongside green fluorescent protein (GFP) libraries of yeast. The team integrates these datasets by standardizing identifiers and mapping orthologous genes across species to combine layers of evidence. To mitigate data heterogeneity, the team tracks covariates at the study level and applies domain adaptation to align features of images.

The timeline includes holding meetings and virtual sprints to deliver a standardized ontology and reproducible workflows without specific dates. Collaboration across laboratories is necessary because the project requires diverse expertise in biology and statistics alongside large computational resources.

The team will release all code and derived datasets under permissive licenses to provide public access to the workflows. The team includes investigators and researchers in their early career across biology and computer science with training opportunities during collaborative sprints.

title: A Pan-Cell Atlas of Cytoskeletal Self-Organization: Integrating Live-Cell Imaging, Proteomics, and Biophysical Models
title_norm: a pancell atlas of cytoskeletal selforganization integrating livecell imaging proteomics and biophysical models
standardized_text:
This project in cell biology and biophysics investigates how molecular components systematically determine the physical organization of the cytoskeleton. Nanoscale interactions generate mesoscale structures but how to integrate disparate datasets to identify general principles of organization remains unknown. This study seeks to identify regulators of cytoskeletal patterns to establish general physical principles of cytoskeletal self organization.

The retrospective design of the study harmonizes public datasets and uses machine learning to align quantitative structural features with molecular data. The team will apply algorithms for image segmentation (Cellpose) and variational autoencoders and biophysical models of active gels. Validation involves testing on cell lines that are held out and comparing inferred parameters against established facts of biology.

The project utilizes the Image Data Resource and Cell Image Library and Broad Institute Cell Painting and datasets of RNAi. The team will integrate these datasets by extracting standardized features from images to align them with proteomic and genetic data. The team will mitigate the limitation of comparing different microscopy modalities by using training that is domain adversarial for batch correction.

The timeline includes virtual sprints on a monthly basis and in person meetings to produce a harmonized table of features. This project of a large scale requires multi lab collaboration because integrating heterogeneous imaging modalities with proteomic data exceeds laboratory capacity.

The team will share all code and workflows that are containerized and the Cytoskeletal Self Organization Atlas through public repositories. The team includes cell biophysicists and graduate students who will receive training through workshops that are hands on and dataset creation.

title: Emergent Chromatin Domains at the Mesoscale: Synthesizing Hi-C, Imaging, and Epigenomic Data to Explain 3D Genome Function
title_norm: emergent chromatin domains at the mesoscale synthesizing hic imaging and epigenomic data to explain 3d genome function
standardized_text:
This study examines three dimensional chromatin folding to understand how mesoscale genomic structures form and why experimental assays yield conflicting results.
Although genomic datasets and mechanistic models exist, the relative contributions of these mechanisms remain unresolved and data remain inconsistently processed.
The primary research question asks how molecular perturbations affect cellular functions to transition correlative observations into predictive rules of genome organization.

The study design is a retrospective synthesis of public data that integrates metadata harmonization with machine learning and mechanistic model calibration.
Key methods include topological domain calling and polymer physics simulations of loop extrusion calibrated through Bayesian optimization and neural network models.
The team validates models using chromosome level cross validation and posterior predictive checks on an open benchmarking suite with imaging constraints.

The project utilizes public datasets from the Image Data Resource and ENCODE including Hi-C and single cell multi omics data.
The team integrates datasets by standardizing metadata and mapping imaging coordinates to genomic reference builds to constrain genomic contact models.
To mitigate assay heterogeneity, the team categorizes datasets into quality tiers and propagates uncertainty using hierarchical statistical models.

The timeline features monthly virtual sprints to deliver key milestones including a standardized data resource and reproducible workflows.
This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in polymer physics and genomics with high performance computational infrastructure.

The team shares harmonized data matrices and publishes reproducible workflows to open source simulation and machine learning repositories.
The team includes researchers from multiple career stages who train graduate students through reproducibility audits and community outreach.

title: A Unified Synthesis of Protein Complex Stoichiometry and Assembly Pathways from Structural, Proteomic, and Ribosome Profiling Data
title_norm: a unified synthesis of protein complex stoichiometry and assembly pathways from structural proteomic and ribosome profiling data
standardized_text:
In cellular biology no unified quantitative framework integrates structural data with proteomic abundance and translation dynamics to predict pathways of assembly. Existing databases provide structural interfaces and protein abundance but isolated analyses leave kinetics and condition specific stoichiometry of protein complexes unknown. This study identifies rules of stoichiometry to explain how cells maintain stability of protein complexes and discover disease associated vulnerabilities.

The proposed study integrates public datasets to build probabilistic models that reconstruct pathways of assembly and predict sensitivity to dosage. Key algorithms include hierarchical Bayesian modeling and Bayesian learning of structure and algorithms for network flow and regularized regression. The team will validate predictions against experimentally characterized protein complexes and perform ablation studies to assess the contribution of each data type.

The study will utilize databases including Protein Data Bank (PDB) and AlphaFold DB and Complex Portal and DepMap and UniProt. The team will integrate datasets by mapping proteins to standardized identifiers and extracting graphs of structural interfaces for probabilistic priors. To mitigate missing structural data, the team will use AlphaFold predictions and manage batch effects in proteomics with hierarchical Bayesian modeling.

Although the chronological timeline is not specified, milestones include establishing pipelines and developing models and releasing the Complex Assembly Atlas. This cross disciplinary project requires collaboration because integrating structural biology and proteomics exceeds the expertise and infrastructure of any single laboratory.

The team will share all data and code and reproducible pipelines through an open access database called the Complex Assembly Atlas. The cross institutional team includes quantitative scientists and domain experts who will train graduate students and postdocs through modeling sprints.

title: Mesoscale Metabolic Channeling: Synthesizing Spatial Proteomics, Metabolomics, and Enzyme Complex Data to Map Functional Microdomains
title_norm: mesoscale metabolic channeling synthesizing spatial proteomics metabolomics and enzyme complex data to map functional microdomains
standardized_text:
This study in systems biology examines how the clustering of enzymes into microdomains affects reactions to resolve a methodological gap. Although individual studies show that enzymes associate to coordinate reactions, the prevalence and quantitative influence of this organization remain unknown. The project investigates how stress alters the clustering of enzymes to resolve discrepancies between levels of enzymes and chemical outputs.

The study design integrates public datasets to construct models of networks and uses machine learning (ML) to predict clustering of enzymes. The team will apply Bayesian statistics and supervised machine learning to identify microdomains and to simulate metabolic reactions. Validation involves comparing predictions against groups of controls and testing simulated rates of reactions against experimental data of metabolic flux.

The project utilizes data from the Human Protein Atlas and the PRIDE archive alongside several other public databases. The team will integrate datasets by converting identifiers into standardized formats and combining features into a single network graph. To mitigate missing data and platform specific biases, the researchers will apply metadata normalization and calculate intervals of confidence for locations.

This project of twenty four months includes standardization of data followed by modeling of networks and validation in the final months. This work requires cross disciplinary collaboration because it demands specialized knowledge in imaging and computational modeling and machine learning.

The team will share findings through a public database and release all computational pipelines and code in open source repositories. The team includes senior researchers and trainees from biochemistry and statistics who will receive specialized instruction in modeling of systems.

Ultimately, these spatial metabolic models will resolve long standing errors in metabolic modeling and explain discrepancies between enzyme levels and actual chemical outputs.

title: Emergent Robustness in Gene Regulatory Networks: A Synthesis of Single-Cell Perturbation Atlases Across Cell Types
title_norm: emergent robustness in gene regulatory networks a synthesis of singlecell perturbation atlases across cell types
standardized_text:
This study examines gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and the stability of cell identities under genetic perturbations to identify universal network structures. Although GRNs maintain stability through feedback and redundancy, the relationship between architecture of GRNs and chromatin state remains unresolved across datasets. This project asks how architectures of GRNs and chromatin states interact to control cellular stability and establish causal regulatory relationships.

This computational synthesis project integrates public single cell perturbation data with molecular priors to infer and align causal GRNs. The team will use scVI and totalVI for data integration alongside graphical models and latent dynamical models for reconstruction of GRNs. The team will validate results using a framework that evaluates network predictions against held out data from perturbations and reference standards.

The study will utilize datasets of single cell perturbations from GEO and scPerturb alongside epigenomic data from ENCODE and STRING. The team will integrate datasets by standardizing metadata and correcting effects of batch using databases of physical interactions as structural constraints. To mitigate heterogeneity and variable efficacies of perturbations, the team will calculate explicit efficacy scores and use algorithms for batch correction.

The project will release a harmonized atlas and a suite for benchmarking, though the specific chronological timeline is not specified. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in genomics of single cells and statistical causal inference and dynamical systems.

The team will share findings and software tools through open source libraries of code and public repositories with permanent digital identifiers. The diverse team spans multiple stages of careers from students to principal investigators and provides training in causal modeling.

title: A Community Synthesis of Mesoscale Protein Quality Control: Integrating Proteostasis Networks, Aggregation Data, and Stress Responses
title_norm: a community synthesis of mesoscale protein quality control integrating proteostasis networks aggregation data and stress responses
standardized_text:
This project investigates quality control of proteins because no framework connects molecular networks to aggregation of proteins and survival of cells. Researchers understand interactions among chaperones and pathways of degradation but do not know how these elements define discrete states of cells. The primary question is whether cells occupy discrete states of proteostasis to establish principles for resilience against stressors in the environment.

The study uses meta analysis to integrate public datasets and apply modeling of latent states to define regimes of proteostasis. The team will apply factor analysis of data from multiple views and dynamic Bayesian models to analyze the integrated datasets. The team will validate models using cross validation and external validation against known perturbations and benchmarking against randomized networks.

The project will use datasets from PRIDE and BioGRID and HuRI and the Gene Expression Omnibus and AlphaFold. The team will integrate datasets by mapping assays of proteomics to a standardized scale and using models of latent variables. To mitigate inconsistent definitions of the solubility of proteins, the team will establish strict standards for metadata and assays.

Milestones of the project include completing curation of data and releasing the atlas although a chronological timeline is not specified. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because integrating diverse modalities of data exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory.

The team will share findings through an open access atlas and publish reproducible workflows and open source software. The team includes researchers across various stages of careers and disciplines who will provide opportunities for training in analysis.

title: Emergent Cell Polarity from Molecular Interactions: Synthesizing Spatial Transcriptomics, Proteomics, and Imaging Across Epithelia
title_norm: emergent cell polarity from molecular interactions synthesizing spatial transcriptomics proteomics and imaging across epithelia
standardized_text:
This study of the biology of epithelial cells addresses the lack of a quantitative framework for spatial polarity. Although molecular regulators are known, current understanding remains limited by a reliance on single modalities of data without spatial context. The project seeks to model how networks of molecules generate spatial polarity to predict how disruptions of structure drive diverse diseases.

The design of the study is a computational synthesis of public datasets using standardized ontologies and modeling of networks. The team will apply segmentation with Markov random fields and alignment of spatial coordinates via eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian. Validation of results will involve testing for consistency across datasets and performing analyses of sensitivity such as ablation of markers.

The project will utilize public datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus and the database of the Human Cell Atlas. Integration of datasets will involve mapping of cell types to ontologies and converting spatial data into graphs of proximity. To address heterogeneity in resolution of data, the project will implement standardized ontologies and apply analyses of sensitivity.

The timeline includes an initial summit on ontologies and the release of the Polarity Synthesis Atlas and Polarity Scoring Toolkit. Collaboration is required because the project spans diverse platforms of data and demands expertise in the biology of epithelial cells.

The team will publish the Polarity Synthesis Atlas and release the Polarity Scoring Toolkit as open source software. The team includes computational scientists and provides funded opportunities for graduate students to participate in workshops on analysis of data.

title: A Synthesis of Mitochondrial Network Emergence: Linking Morphodynamics, Proteostasis, and Bioenergetics Across Cell Types
title_norm: a synthesis of mitochondrial network emergence linking morphodynamics proteostasis and bioenergetics across cell types
standardized_text:

title: Synthesizing the Emergent Assembly of Bacterial Microcompartments
title_norm: synthesizing the emergent assembly of bacterial microcompartments
standardized_text:

The team applies software for structural prediction and graph neural networks alongside reinforcement learning and algorithms for phase separation. This project utilizes the NCBI RefSeq database and the Protein Data Bank (PDB) alongside the public PRIDE database. The team integrates data by mapping sequences of genes to models of structures and parameterizing kinetic simulations with data from proteomics. Computational tools for prediction estimate missing structural details, while automated pipelines for data cleaning resolve inconsistencies across databases.

Although a chronological timeline is not provided, milestones of the project include creating a unified database and developing predictive models. Combining structural biology and microbiology with biophysics and machine learning exceeds the technical capabilities of any single laboratory.

title: Temporal Emergence in Protein Interaction Networks: Synthesizing Dynamic Interactomics Across Cell Cycle, Circadian, and Stress Response Programs

title: Emergent Properties of the Cellular Crowding Landscape: Synthesizing Biophysical, Structural, and Systems Data to Understand Macromolecular Organization

standardized_text:

The project maps cytoplasmic density variations to link molecular physics with organization at the cellular scale and clarify mechanisms of protein aggregation.

The study design integrates structural and proteomics data to map subcellular density and trains machine learning (ML) models on biophysical measurements. The team applies Voronoi tessellation and calculations of solvent accessible surfaces and Bayesian hierarchical modeling and agent based simulations. Validation of results involves independent datasets and analyses of sensitivity and cross validation across species and experimental testing of predictions.

The project utilizes PaxDb and PRIDE and the Protein Data Bank and the AlphaFold Database and the Human Protein Atlas. The team integrates datasets by standardizing identifiers of proteins and calculating molecular volumes and predicting subcellular localization with machine learning. Because uncertainties of measurements and experimental discrepancies exist, the team uses Bayesian hierarchical models to propagate errors and identify robust predictions.

Over three years the milestones of the project include biannual meetings of working groups and the release of a database and software. This project requires collaboration across multiple laboratories to combine diverse expertise and access computational resources beyond a single laboratory.

The team shares all findings and workflows for analysis publicly through the version controlled repositories of containerized code. The team of biophysicists and computational scientists at various stages of careers provides opportunities for training and research during summer for undergraduates.

title: The Emergence of Ribosome Heterogeneity: Synthesizing Structural, Compositional, and Translational Data to Understand Specialized Ribosomes

title: Emergent Properties of the Nuclear Pore Complex: Integrating Structural, Transport, and Regulatory Data Across Scales
title_norm: emergent properties of the nuclear pore complex integrating structural transport and regulatory data across scales
standardized_text:
The proposed study investigates the physical structure of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) because its collective transport mechanisms remain unknown. Researchers understand the protein composition of the NPC but separate datasets do not explain the physical mechanisms of transport. The primary question is how the spatial arrangement of NPC proteins regulates transport to identify the physical mechanisms of genetic diseases.

The proposed study uses a computational design for data synthesis to integrate existing datasets into unified physical models of the NPC. The project will apply coarse grained molecular dynamics and the Integrative Modeling Platform alongside machine learning and statistical network analysis. The team will validate the computational models by testing predictions against experimental data and generating hypotheses for future laboratory experiments.

The study will use data from the Protein Data Bank and the AlphaFold Database and the Gene Expression Omnibus. Automated pipelines for extraction and the Integrative Modeling Platform will integrate these datasets using standardized biological ontologies to ensure data compatibility. Because existing datasets are fragmented and inconsistent, the project will use Bayesian inference and quantification of uncertainty within the structural models.

Over a three year period the project will establish collaborative meetings and develop a database to construct models and publish hypotheses. Because combining structural biology and genomics exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory, this project requires cross disciplinary collaboration.

The team will share all code through repositories for version control and publish findings in open access journals for public availability. Computational biologists from six institutions and early career scientists will offer training through rotations of students and workshops.

title: The Emergence of Cellular Memory: Synthesizing Epigenetic, Transcriptional, and Chromatin Data to Understand Heritable Cell States
title_norm: the emergence of cellular memory synthesizing epigenetic transcriptional and chromatin data to understand heritable cell states
standardized_text:
This research of cellular memory addresses how transcription factors and chromatin modifications integrate to maintain stable identities across cell divisions. Although chromatin structure and DNA methylation regulate gene expression, how these systems interact to preserve cell identity remains unknown. The project will construct models of cell stability to explain developmental decisions and understand memory disruptions in cancer.

The study design features a computational synthesis of public genomic datasets using standardized processing pipelines and machine learning models. Key methods include modeling of chromatin states and analysis of pseudotime trajectories alongside machine learning algorithms like deep neural networks. The team will validate results through cross validation across cell types and temporal validation of developmental time series data.

The project utilizes ChIP-seq data from ENCODE and single cell transcriptomics from the Human Cell Atlas and Hi-C data. The team will integrate datasets by aligning genomic coordinates and mapping epigenetic marks to standardized annotations of the genome. The proposed study does not address information regarding known limitations of the data or specific plans for mitigation.

The project is planned for a duration of three years although the proposal does not specify intermediate milestones. Cross disciplinary collaboration is necessary because integrating diverse datasets requires combined expertise in chromatin biology and computational science.

The project will share findings through open access publications and host the Integrated Cellular Memory Database for public use. The team includes biologists from various career stages and offers training opportunities such as workshops for data analysis.

standardized_text:

To mitigate limitations of data, the team will model missing structures using AlphaFold2 and filter databases of interactions by evidence codes.

The team will share all code via GitHub and publish findings in journals with open access to ensure public accessibility. The team includes researchers from seven institutions across various stages of careers and offers opportunities for training of students.

title: Emergent Properties of the Glycocalyx: Synthesizing Glycomic, Proteomic, and Functional Data to Understand Cell Surface Organization
title_norm: emergent properties of the glycocalyx synthesizing glycomic proteomic and functional data to understand cell surface organization
standardized_text:

Although individual carbohydrate structures are documented in separate databases, these resources remain unintegrated and the physical organization is unresolved. This project integrates public datasets to model the three dimensional structure of the cell coat and predict molecular control of cellular functions.

The computational design progresses from mapping molecular composition to simulating physical structures and training machine learning models of biological activities. The project applies network analysis, trajectory modeling, coarse grained physical simulations, and supervised machine learning algorithms such as neural networks. Physical models are compared against published biophysical measurements and machine learning predictions are validated using independent test datasets.

The project utilizes data from GlyGen, GlyTouCan, UniCarb DB, the Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, ProteomeXchange, PRIDE, and Gene Expression Omnibus. The team integrates these resources by converting carbohydrate nomenclatures into standardized formats and combining structural and abundance data into unified matrices. Inconsistencies in data formats and naming conventions across databases are resolved using automated translation software and standardized metadata guidelines.

Over a three year period, the project will establish collaborative computational workflows, host annual meetings, and deliver a public database. The project requires a multi laboratory effort because the necessary expertise spans carbohydrate chemistry, cell biology, structural biology, and computer science.

All databases, simulation models, and software tools will be made publicly available and code will be shared using containerized packages. The team includes scientists from six institutions representing multiple career stages and will offer training through student rotations and workshops.

title: The Emergence of Enhancer-Promoter Specificity: Synthesizing Chromatin, Transcription, and 3D Genome Data
title_norm: the emergence of enhancerpromoter specificity synthesizing chromatin transcription and 3d genome data
standardized_text:
In gene regulation it is unknown how multiple molecular factors interact to determine specificity of communication between enhancers and promoters. Although enhancers regulate distant genes through chromatin looping, understanding of how these components integrate to establish specificity remains incomplete. The primary objective is to determine how specificity arises from integrated features to improve predictions of the effects of mutations.

The proposed study uses a three part computational synthesis of public data to map and predict connections between enhancers and promoters. The team will apply machine learning (ML) models and algorithms for calling interactions (FitHiC2) to analyze features and predict connections. Validation of results will involve a held out test set and external validation using expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data.

The project will use public datasets from ENCODE and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) containing genomic and eQTL data. The team will integrate datasets by mapping all data to the GRCh38 reference genome and extracting features into unified matrices. Because technical variability exists across consortia, the team will implement standardized workflows and apply strict thresholds for quality control.

The three year project will deliver an integrated database of connections alongside predictive models and testable experimental hypotheses. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because integrating massive multi omic datasets exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory.

The team will publicly release all generated resources including the integrated database of connections and containerized workflows for analysis. The diverse team spans multiple stages of careers and institutions to provide opportunities for training including workshops and research experiences.

title: Decoding the Emergent Organization of the Endoplasmic Reticulum: Multi-Scale Synthesis of Structure, Function, and Dynamics
title_norm: decoding the emergent organization of the endoplasmic reticulum multiscale synthesis of structure function and dynamics
standardized_text:

The study uses a computational pipeline to integrate diverse datasets into Bayesian frameworks and models of multi layer networks. Key methods include machine learning and segmentation of images for cryo electron tomography (cryo-ET) implemented in Python and R. The team will validate results by testing models on held out datasets and comparing predictions with published experimental data.

The study will source datasets of proteomics and lipidomics from public databases including PRIDE and LIPID MAPS and EMDB. The team will integrate datasets by correlating spatial lipidomics with proteomic maps and linking structural measurements to molecular composition. To mitigate heterogeneity of data, the team will apply standards of quality control and use Bayesian frameworks to quantify uncertainty.

Milestones for Year 1 include collection of data while Year 2 milestones focus on construction of the database. The project requires collaboration across disciplines because no single laboratory possesses the diverse expertise needed to integrate multi scale data.

The team will share findings through publications with open access and host code on GitHub to support open science. The team includes faculty in early stages of their careers and will train graduate students in cell biology.

title: Oceans of Disorder: Elucidating the Role of Disordered Proteins in Cellular Adaptation

standardized_text:

Key tools include AlphaFold3 for prediction of structure and LAMMPS for simulations of molecular dynamics alongside architectures of deep learning. title: From image data and biophysical simulations to principles of mesoscale organization through integrated transfer learning

title: Searching the crosslinking mass spectrometry universe for new protein-protein interactions

This scope requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in mass spectrometry, structural biology, standardization of data and engineering of databases.

title: From Protein Knots to Pierced Lassos: Unraveling the Evolutionary Origin of Complex Topologies
title_norm: from protein knots to pierced lassos unraveling the evolutionary origin of complex topologies
standardized_text:
Structural biology lacks understanding of when and how proteins with complex entangled three dimensional shapes first appeared during evolution. Researchers have identified structural similarities between knotted and unknotted proteins but existing databases do not pinpoint exact evolutionary branch points. The project identifies evolutionary branch points of entangled shapes to establish a framework that may reveal new therapeutic targets.

The study analyzes nine knotted and 26 families of lasso proteins by mapping structural shapes onto reconstructed evolutionary trees. The team applies phylogenetic reconstruction and structural modeling using machine learning based on sequences with AlphaLasso and KnotProt 2.0. The team compares structural predictions against verified annotations of families and tests functional impacts against experimental data from deep mutational scanning.

The project utilizes diverse databases including UniProt and the Protein Data Bank (PDB) to gather data on structure and evolution. The team integrates data on sequences and structures to build phylogenetic trees with functional annotations mapped at the amino acid level. To address scarce physical structures, the project uses models of artificial intelligence and high performance computing to simulate missing transition points.

The 24 month project spans five phases that include integration of data and structural modeling and two scientific publications. The project requires expertise across disciplines in evolutionary biology and structural modeling alongside computational resources that exceed a single laboratory.

The team will share findings through two peer reviewed publications and establish an open access platform for studying protein entanglement. The team includes an expert in evolutionary analysis and a student researcher alongside structural specialists and a staff scientist.

title: Deciphering systemic biological networks through AI-driven multi-omic integration
title_norm: deciphering systemic biological networks through aidriven multiomic integration
standardized_text:
This study in systemic physiology examines molecular networks across organs to determine how inter organ communication is structured and regulated. Organs communicate via signaling molecules to maintain homeostasis but global coordination across the whole organism remains unclear due to inconsistent datasets. The project will map these networks to build a computational model that predicts systemic responses and reduces animal testing.

The design of the study integrates multi omic data within and across organs to build a dynamic computational model. Key methods include a graph network model of reaction diffusion with a graph Laplacian operator and digital twin simulation modeling. Model predictions of molecular states will be validated against empirical measurements from physical animals to guide subsequent in vivo experiments.

The project uses the Molecular Transducers of Physical Activity Consortium (MoTrPAC) dataset containing multi omic data from eighteen tissues of rats. Datasets will be integrated vertically within each organ and horizontally across organs using a network model based on physical connectivity. To mitigate data scarcity and inconsistency, the team uses standardized data from the same animals and a hybrid approach to modeling.

Milestones for year one include integration of a single organ while year two focuses on mapping interactions of multiple organs. Cross disciplinary collaboration is required because the biological lead lacks expertise in bioinformatics and machine learning and data science.

The team will share findings through publications in journals but plans for sharing of data with open access are not specified. The team includes biological and computational researchers but stages of careers and opportunities for training are not specified.

title: Conserved Disorder: Learning Sequence Conservation from Functional Constraints in Intrinsically Disordered Regions
title_norm: conserved disorder learning sequence conservation from functional constraints in intrinsically disordered regions
standardized_text:
This study in structural biology and bioinformatics investigates how physical properties preserve the functions of rapidly mutating disordered regions of proteins. Although structured domains show clear conservation, existing annotations are biased toward them while disordered regions mutate rapidly and vary in sequence. The primary objective is to identify conserved disordered regions to establish a foundational framework for annotating their biological functions.

The proposed study combines the integration of databases and simulations of molecular dynamics and machine learning (ML) to compare disordered regions. The project applies software for prediction of disorder and simulations of molecular dynamics and ML to integrate structural descriptors. The team will validate results by testing accuracy of the ML model on new sequences and using databases to verify conservation.

The study will utilize datasets from UniProt, Eukaryotic Linear Motif, IDRome, MaveDB, GISAID, MobiDB, ProteinGym, ClinVar, PhosphoSitePlus, OrthoDB and Ensembl. The team will integrate these datasets by mapping structural motifs and sites of post translational modification and mutational data onto sequences. To mitigate potential gaps in primary datasets, the team will use alternative databases for predictions and mutational variants.

The two year timeline includes curation of the database in months one to six and completing simulations by month twenty four. This project requires collaboration across disciplines to combine expertise in biophysics and bioinformatics and simulations across three laboratories.

The team will share findings through a database with open access to conserved regions and reproducible computational workflows. The team comprises principal investigators from three laboratories and staff scientists and trainees receiving interdisciplinary instruction in biophysics.

title: Integrative Multi-Omics Synthesis to Identify Shared Molecular Mechanisms of Mammalian Hibernation
title_norm: integrative multiomics synthesis to identify shared molecular mechanisms of mammalian hibernation
standardized_text:
This project examines the molecular mechanisms of mammalian hibernation to determine if shared transcriptional pathways govern suppression of metabolism across species. Hibernation involves reductions of temperature and metabolism but conserved pathways across lineages remain unresolved without an evolutionary context. The study identifies conserved genes for suppression of metabolism to understand evolutionary adaptations which may inform treatments for human conditions.

The design involves comparative meta analysis of public data from ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing across tissues of diverse species. The team applies tools including STAR and OrthoFinder alongside Ornstein-Uhlenbeck models and a newly developed bivariate model of trait evolution. Simulations will validate the newly developed evolutionary models and the corrected Akaike Information Criterion will guide selection of models.

The project utilizes public datasets of RNA sequencing from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Short Read Archive. The team integrates datasets by mapping raw reads of sequences to reference genomes and establishing orthology of genes using comparative models. To mitigate sparse data and inconsistent sampling of tissues, the team will develop analytical models within a phylogenetic framework.

The two year timeline includes mapping of sequences and development of models followed by biological interpretation and preparation of the manuscript. This project requires multi lab collaboration because integrating genomic datasets across species demands diverse expertise that exceeds a single laboratory.

The team will release developed software as open source code and publish a public dataset of hibernation studies. The team includes researchers at various stages of careers across disciplines and provides training for a Staff Scientist Assistant.

title: Revealing the Ontology of Allostery through Community-Scale Synthesis
title_norm: revealing the ontology of allostery through communityscale synthesis
standardized_text:
This study investigates allostery of proteins in transporters to resolve unknown features that distinguish regulated proteins from non regulated counterparts. Databases document some proteins regulated by external stimuli but they lack negative examples and the mechanisms of differentiation remain unknown. This project compares homologs of transporters to identify allosteric sites and evolutionary origins using negative controls to annotate new systems.

The proposed study curates a database of transporters using insertion of domains as a proxy to perform comparative analyses. The proposed study applies neural networks and molecular dynamics using tools that include AlphaFold and PyTorch and HMMER. Validation involves assessing the predictive accuracy of models in distinguishing allosteric proteins and identifying key residues and proposing mutations.

The project will utilize datasets from the Allosteric Database and Transport Protein Data Base and MAVEdb and UniProt. These datasets will be integrated into a new database containing alignments of sequences and structures for fifty families of proteins. To address sparsity of data, the team will use insertion of domains as a proxy and mine literature using artificial intelligence.

The two year timeline includes identification of datasets and curation of data followed by generation of models and delivery of tools. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration to combine expertise in machine learning and biophysics of proteins to analyze large datasets.

The database will be made publicly available through the CyVerse/NCEMS platform and findings will be shared through peer reviewed publications. The team includes researchers from chemistry of materials and computational biology but stages of careers and training are not specified.

title: SynEvo: Discovering Evolutionary Principles of Molecular Organization through Cross-Species Data Synthesis
title_norm: synevo discovering evolutionary principles of molecular organization through crossspecies data synthesis
standardized_text:
Evolutionary systems biology lacks a framework for synthesis to explain how evolutionary forces shape mesoscale molecular organization in humans and mosquitoes. Although datasets of multi omics and comparative genomic models exist, no method combines population genetic variation across species using mechanistic models. The study will develop a framework for machine learning (ML) to identify conserved modules and reveal evolutionary principles of networks.

The design of the study harmonizes multi omics data to train hybrid ML models and align manifolds across species. The team will apply graph neural networks and variational autoencoders and metabolic models at genome scale and tools for balancing flux. The team will validate results using evolutionary simulators and cross validation and comparisons of modules with transcriptomic and metabolomic data.

The project will use datasets of genomics and metabolomics from public GTEx and All of Us and TOPMed and VectorBase repositories. Datasets will be integrated through a standardized pipeline for normalization and jointly mapped across species using models of ML. To mitigate sparse genetic variants of mosquitoes, the team will restrict imputation and prioritize analyses focused on humans if alignment issues arise.

The timeline of two years includes deploying the integrator of data and training hybrid models and releasing the atlas of molecules. This project requires collaboration across disciplines to combine diverse expertise in ML and metabolic modeling and population genetics of mosquitoes.

The team will release workflows with version control and hybrid models and the interactive atlas in public repositories with online tutorials. Three lead researchers and staff for support will manage the project while providing opportunities for academic training of graduate and undergraduate students.

title: A Unified Framework for Analyses of Proteome Turnover Dynamics
title_norm: a unified framework for analyses of proteome turnover dynamics
standardized_text:
This biochemistry and evolutionary biology project investigates protein turnover across domains of life to address unknown determinants of protein lifetimes. Although some degradation pathways are conserved, global comparisons of protein stability and quantitative influences on lifetimes remain unknown. The study asks how protein stability is conserved across kingdoms to establish the first unified database of protein turnover.

The design integrates public datasets of protein turnover for four species with structural features using machine learning (ML) models. Key methods include decay kinetic models and deep neural networks with cross attention mechanisms for analysis of sequence embeddings. The team will validate results by measuring reconstruction loss and comparing prediction accuracy against baseline databases of degradation signals.

The study utilizes datasets of mass spectrometry from PRIDE and orthology data from OrthoDB and structural predictions from AlphaFold. The team will integrate these data by mapping orthologous proteins and merging turnover rates with structural and pathway annotations. To mitigate inconsistencies in data formats, the team will reanalyze all raw data using a unified computational pipeline.

The twenty four month timeline includes cataloging datasets and mapping orthologs and releasing the final database and pipeline. This project requires cross disciplinary collaboration because it combines experimental proteomics with computational biology and analysis of evolutionary systems.

The team will share all data and code on GitHub and CyVerse and publish findings in open access journals. Principal investigators and staff scientists compose the team and other career stages and training opportunities are not specified.

title: Predictive Synthesis Framework for Elucidating Biophysical Cell State from Spatial Transcriptomics and Proteomics
title_norm: predictive synthesis framework for elucidating biophysical cell state from spatial transcriptomics and proteomics
standardized_text:
Spatial omics lacks methods to integrate the localization of ribonucleic acid (RNA) and proteins to explain cell behavior. Subcellular localization influences cell function but alignment difficulties and a lack of workflows prevent comparison of different molecular modalities. This study asks if spatial patterns predict cell states better than abundance to link molecular distribution directly to cellular phenotypes.

The team will develop an open source pipeline to register tissue sections and train models to predict cell fate. title: Integrating AI and Molecular Dynamics Simulations for Quantitative Prediction of Enzyme Functions

standardized_text:

Trajectories of multi scale simulations and biophysical properties will be integrated into unified embeddings using a module of gated fusion. Insufficient conformational sampling in simulations will be mitigated by using coarse grained models and generative AI and enhanced methods of sampling.

Trajectories and biophysical properties from UniProt, SwissProt, the Protein Data Bank, ATLAS, and mdCATH will be integrated into unified embeddings using a gated fusion module and multimodal machine learning techniques. This framework will move protein modeling beyond static representations by incorporating temporal resolution, which is expected to improve the design of therapeutic and functional biomolecules.

abstract_text: Bacterial organelles representing three distinct structural classes regulate critical cellular processes, making the study of their occurrence, diversity, and interactions within the human gut microbiome essential for understanding microbial physiology. However, the regulation, ecological roles, and community interactions of these organelles remain uncharacterized, and the systematic distribution of condensate forming proteins in bacteria is currently not understood. This project will map organelle prevalence, diversity, and regulation in the gut microbiome using a computational multi omics synthesis approach that will apply HMMER, the Phaseek machine learning model, and weighted gene co expression network analysis. Metagenomic, metatranscriptomic, and metaproteomic datasets from the GMrepo and Inflammatory Bowel Disease databases will be harmonized and paired at the individual sample level to track organelle activity over time. These systematic maps of organelle regulation and distribution in complex communities will ultimately advance the understanding of cellular evolution and inform future synthetic biology applications.
